newsitem.title: DENMARK: Borealis starts 1997 well, outlook tricky.
newsitem.headline: Borealis starts 1997 well, outlook tricky.

text.p: Petrochemicals firm Borealis, which on Wednesday reported a sharp fall in 1996 profits, said that 1997 had started better but that the market outlook remained uncertain and it could not forecast the outcome.
Borealis, owned by Finland's Neste Oy and Norwegian state-owned Statoil, posted 1996 pre-tax profit of 870 million Danish crowns, down from 2.63 billion in 1995.

"1997 started better than 1996, prices for polyolefins are significantly higher and there has been some decline already in the price of crude oil, our most important fuel stock," Borealis chief financial officer Svein Rennemo told Reuters.
"But we think that later in the year new production capacity for polyolefins may come on stream which may undermine the present strength in markets, making the outlook less promising," he said.
Rennemo described the market situation as "sensitive" but said that Borealis was continuing at full speed in its efforts to improve cost-effectiveness.
"As you know we are in a very cyclical industry. If you look upon prices and margins from 1995 to 1996, they reduced our pre-tax profits by up to 2.5 billion Danish crowns," he said.
"It means that we had an on-the-line improvement in profitability if you abstract from the market impact," he said.
Borealis' 1996 net sales fell to 15.6 billion crowns from 17.6 billion the year before and the operating profit fell to 790 million crowns last year from 2.9 billion in 1995, it said.

Finnish and Norwegian-owned Borealis has its headquarters in Copenhagen for communications and tax reasons and because of Denmark's location halfway between its main production sites in Scandinavia and Belgium and Portugal, he said.
The company is Europe's biggest polyolefins maker.
Rennemo said that he was unable to comment on reports that half-owner Neste was talking to several potential buyers for its stake in Borealis.
